title: runtime-cross-cutting-investigation-cookbook
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Overview

This cookbook collects cross-cutting investigation patterns used by the serving runtime team when incidents, regressions, or unexpected cost/latency changes span multiple subsystems (runtime architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling, benchmarking). It is intended for oncall, incident commanders, and engineers performing post-incident diagnostics. Follow the numbered procedures first; use the lookup tables and runbook snippets as shortcuts once familiar.

Key goals
- Rapidly triage impact vs root cause (latency SLO, error surface, cost delta).
- Preserve reproducible artifacts: traces, kernel profiles, synthetic replays.
- Provide a deterministic experiment matrix for validation (benchmarks + microtraces).

Pre-flight checklist (before you start)
- Confirm SLOs impacted and timeframe (10m/1h/24h). Typical SLOs: p95 <= 180ms, p99 <= 500ms for short prompt tier; throughput SLOs: 50 reqs/s per GPU pool.
- Capture a preserved span from distributed tracing covering router -> dispatcher -> kernel layer -> GPU.
- Lock configuration state for the timeframe: scheduler policies, kernel-version, model-variant, quantization profile, admission controller settings.
- Notify stakeholders: oncall lead, runtime owner, product oncall if customer-visible.

1) Rapid impact assessment (10–20 minutes)
1.1 Gather high-level signals
- Console: per-route latency change, token-level cost deltas.
- Telemetry: compute p50/p95/p99 deltas, error-rate change, queue length and slot occupancy.
- Billing signal: per-token cost change (if available).

1.2 Quick hypothesis mapping
Use the Signal -> Likely subsystem mapping (lookup table below) to generate 1–3 initial hypotheses. Prioritize by impact and reversibility.

2) Focused evidence collection (20–60 minutes)
2.1 Traces and causal spans
- Export a 10–30 minute trace window containing both normal and degraded requests. Annotate the span with request prototype (length, model, priority).
- Query example (internal trace UI): "service=kernel AND duration>100ms AND model=~'gpt-.*' | group_by(kernel_variant, node)"

2.2 Kernel profiling snapshot
- Collect one full kernel snapshot from an affected node: kernel traces (per-invocation micro-timeline), GPU occupancy, tensor core utilization, memory high-water marks.
- Commands (operator shell):
  - curl http://node.internal:1234/debug/kernel_snapshot?since=2026-11-05T10:00:00Z -o kernel-snap.json
  - rd-prof collect --node node-42 --duration 30s --output /tmp/kernel-prof.tgz

2.3 Scheduler and admission controller logs
- Pull last 500 scheduler decisions and admission controller responses for the pool. Look for sudden credit depletion, priority inversion, or policy churn.

2.4 Reproduce with microbenchmarks
- Use the microbenchmark runner to replay representative requests (same token lengths and model variant) against a shadow pool. Run three variants: (A) current production config, (B) previous kernel version, (C) previous scheduler policy. Compare p95/p99 and tail-samples.
- Commands:
  - bench-runner --profile replay-corpus.json --pool shadow-a --iterations 200

3) Isolation matrix (experiment plan)
- Change only one variable per experiment. Record the exact state and artifacts. Example matrix rows:
  - baseline (prod config)
  - kernel-old vs kernel-new
  - scheduler-policy-A vs policy-B
  - quantization-profile (int8 vs int4)
  - admission-controller thresholds (slot-limit +/- 10%)
- Record: synthetic traffic, observed trace, kernel snapshot, scheduler log extract.

Lookup table: signal -> probable root causes -> immediate mitigations
- sudden p99 spike + stable p50: probable root causes: rare kernel slow path (tensor core fallback), intermittent GPU thermal throttling, long KV cache misses. Immediate mitigations: route to a fallback model-variant, increase warmstart slots, enable short-circuit FPGA (if available).
- uniform latency increase across fleet: probable root causes: global config change (scheduler/admission), upstream router change, network fabric regression. Immediate mitigations: roll back recent policy change, shift traffic to unaffected region.
- increase in kernel queue length + drop in throughput: probable root causes: credit exhaustion, NUMA-induced memory pressure, preemption storm. Immediate mitigations: reduce admission rate, disable opportunistic preemption, scale up slot pool.
- token-level cost spike without latency changes: probable root causes: model variant upgrade with higher per-token cost, decoding beam-width change, tokenizer mis-configuration. Immediate mitigations: pin model version, revert decoding params.

Runbook snippets (quick actions)
- Eviction / warmstart play (fast, reversible)
  1) Identify hot nodes: telemetry shows >90% occupancy and >100ms extra scheduling delay.
  2) Drain new high-cost tenants via router tag: curl -X POST http://router/api/drain -d '{"tenant":"X"}'
  3) Trigger warmstart on replacement nodes: rd-runtime warmstart --pool pool-A --targets 3
  4) Monitor p95 and kernel error-rate for 15 minutes.

- Scheduler rollback (config-level)
  1) Check recent config commits: git log deploys/scheduler | head -n 10
  2) Apply previous policy (immutable snapshot id): rd-config apply --policy-id p-2026-10-21
  3) Monitor admission decisions and CPU wait times.

Telemetry and observability queries (examples)
- Kernel invocation latency by variant: metrics.query("kernel.invocation.latency{variant:*,model:*}").aggregate(quantiles=[50,95,99])
- Scheduler credit burn-down: metrics.query("scheduler.credit.delta{pool:pool-A}").rollup('1m')
- Trace correlation: select trace_id from spans where service='scheduler' and tag.key='decision' and tag.value='preempt'

Benchmarking integration (when to call the bench team)
- If microbenchmarks cannot reproduce the observed tail behavior within +/-10% at the same configuration, escalate to bench team. Provide: preserved trace window, kernel snapshot, sample inputs, and experiment matrix.
- Bench team checklist: run hardware-matched synthetic replay, run metrics correlation (scheduler vs kernel), and run stress for 2x production QPS for 30m.

Decision ledger (record what you change)
- Always create a short decision artifact stored in /incidents/<id>/decision.yaml with fields: who, why, start_time, end_time, actions, rollback_plan, confidence. Example line (as text): "action: rollback-scheduler-to-p-2026-10-21; who: Aisha; start: 2026-11-05T11:03:00Z; confidence: 0.65"

Post-incident: reproducibility recipe
- Reconstruct the exact experiment using the preserved inputs and pinned binaries (kernel-image hash, scheduler-policy id).
- Run three round-trip reproductions and collect: benchmark report, kernel profile tarball, scheduler decision log, and end-to-end trace. Attach to postmortem.

Appendix: common diagnostic heuristics
- "Kernel-only" signature: per-invocation timeline shows a long window inside the GPU kernel with high tensor-core idle time and memory copy stalls.
- "Scheduler-only" signature: spikes coincide with repeated admission-controller rejects and a diverging credit-accounting curve.
- "Network/IO" signature: long wait times in dispatcher->kernel RPCs, with socket retransmits observed.

Table: artifact types and retention (text table)
- artifact_type | retention | who-keeps
- trace_window (10–60m) | 90 days | runtime-oncall
- kernel-profile (snapshot) | 30 days | infra-team
- bench-report | 365 days | perf-team

Ownership and maintenance
- Owner: runtime reliability team (oncall rotation). Review cadence: quarterly.
- How to propose changes: open PR against this document in the docs repo (docs/eng-serving-runtime/team-wiki) and add at least one reviewer from bench and one from kernel-scheduling.

Contact
- For immediate escalation: oncall@redwood.com and runtime-reliability slack channel (#runtime-reliability).
